title: Decentralization, Privacy, and Everything Between
content:
<p>This post is a combination of at least <em>three</em> different posts I intended to
write and publish over the past year. They inevitably came to the similar
conclusions and it makes sense. In my mind, decentralization and privacy are
mutually beneficial. In the wake of exposure to privacy violations by Google,
Facebook, &amp;c to the general public, it seemed like now would be a great time
to share my thoughts.</p>
<h2>Privacy</h2>
<blockquote>
<p>If you are not paying for it, you&#39;re not the customer; you&#39;re the product
being sold. — Andrew Lewis (blue_beetle)<a href="https://www.metafilter.com/95152/Userdriven-discontent#3256046">1</a></p>
</blockquote>
<p>This oft-referenced quote was posted on MetaFilter on August 26th, 2010. It&#39;s
been nearly a decade since then and clearly, that quote is timeless. The
increasingly parasitic advertising industry is fed by a never-ending supply of
user-data gathered and sold by almost every ̶o̶n̶l̶i̶n̶e̶ o̶f̶f̶l̶i̶n̶e̶ service. Oh yeah,
that&#39;s right; you can be tracked o̶f̶f̶l̶i̶n̶e̶. The data gatherers are your usual
suspects: Facebook, Google, Twitter, as well as unknown data brokers of which
new ones are launching seemingly weekly. Have you looked at the blacklist of
your favorite ad blocker? It&#39;s a <em>mess</em>.</p>
<p>The aforementioned data gatherers are in the business of keeping your
attention. The visual redesigns, additional features, and so on are not
created to make a better product for your perusal. Oh no, these changes are
A/B tested and analyzed to ensure that you spend as much time using those
products as possible. Why? So that app can send usage data and patterns back
to the mothership to collect your info to update their algorithms and sell to
advertisers for a pretty penny and the cycle continues.</p>
<p>Before this year, casual Internet users would roll their eyes at everything
I&#39;ve said thus far, <code>¯\_(ツ)_/¯</code>, and say something inane like, &quot;It is what it
is.&quot; or, &quot;I have nothing to hide.&quot;</p>
<blockquote>
<p>Arguing that you don&#39;t care about the right to privacy because you have
nothing to hide is no different than saying you don&#39;t care about free speech
because you have nothing to say. — Edward Snowden</p>
</blockquote>
<p>Frustrating as those eye rolls may be, you cannot force someone to care about
something <em>you</em> think is important. I&#39;ve been harping on about privacy to my
friends for years and some of them are starting to come around. The tech (and
mainstream) media&#39;s continued coverage about the evils of (mostly) Facebook
and Google has become a roar too loud to ignore.</p>
<p>FINALLY.</p>
<p>People have realized (or are starting to realize) that they can no longer
depend on the kindness of corporations offering free things on the Internet…
when you think of it that way, it&#39;s kind of surprising that we would think
there wouldn&#39;t be strings attached. Huh. Anyhoo, getting away from Facebook is
<em>relatively</em> easy. Ironically, if you have a lot of relatives on the platform,
leaving is quite difficult.</p>
<h2>Cancel Facebook</h2>
<p>Your entrenchment level with Facebook varies with the next person and most
likely with me too. I&#39;ll share what I did leading up to and after my leave
from Facebook in 2016.</p>
<ol>
<li>I requested a backup of my data.</li>
<li>After downloading my data, I went to my profile page and spent a couple
days deleting posts. This was tedious as hell and I never actually
finished. I think I got through my first three years and then my recent two
years before calling it quits with that task.</li>
<li>I also deleted integrations with other services and took the time to delete
accounts with services I barely remembered using prior the integration
deletion.</li>
<li>I told close friends, family, and my girlfriend (now wife) my plans and why
I was doing so. I have several family members on Facebook but I also own a
phone. I had zero interest with staying in contact with people I knew from
high school, those were all passive &quot;friendships&quot; at that point.</li>
</ol>
<h2>Cancel Google</h2>
<p>Hoo boy, this one&#39;s a <em>doozy</em>. Entire livelihoods, businesses, and lifestyles
rely on Google in some shape or form…especially if your daily mobile driver
is an Android device. I grew weary of Google long before my divorce from
Facebook and I found an email replacement in Mail-in-a-Box<a href="https://mailinabox.email">2</a>, a self-hosted
email solution that also has calendar and address book capabilities. For
search, I use DuckDuckGo<a href="https://duckduckgo.com">3</a>. I&#39;m on iOS/macOS so Apple Maps is a suitable
Google Maps replacement for me (btw, Apple Maps is <em>fantastic</em> in Japan).</p>
<p>At this point in time, YouTube is nigh-impossible to replace. Nintendo
doesn&#39;t upload their videos to Vimeo. MKBHD or any other super profitable
YouTube creator isn&#39;t leaving the platform anytime soon either so it&#39;s a total
crapshoot. I&#39;m no longer logged-in to YouTube but I still get email
notifications when a channel I&#39;m interested in uploads a video. For videos I
<em>really</em> want to see again, I download them with youtube-dl<a href="https://rg3.github.io/youtube-dl">4</a>, an awesome
command line program that is capable of downloading videos from pretty much
any video sharing site (not just YouTube). Here&#39;s my configuration file
(located at <code>~/.config/youtube-dl/config</code>):</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">-f bestvideo+bestaudio
-o ~/Movies/%(title)s.%(ext)s
</code></pre>
<p>It automatically downloads the best audio and best video sources for whatever
video URL you supply and combines them to create a single file. That file then
gets saved to my <code>~/Movies</code> folder. I alias the <code>youtube-dl</code> command in my
<code>.zshrc</code> config so I can type <code>yt</code> followed by a URL for a super-quick
workflow.</p>
<p>Unfortunately, Google Apps for Work exists and that means I have not fully
escaped their ecosystem. When it comes to most businesses, familiarity and
cost-savings often take precedence over ideals. Make no mistake, finding
(worthy) alternatives to every single one of Google&#39;s offerings is expensive
in either time spent searching or cost for a single app. Sometimes both!
However, I think the upfront cost is worth the longtime gain. You will have to
be careful though. There is no shortage of startups with compelling products
that are merely skins on top of Google&#39;s existing services (last year I
interviewed for such a company that I thought was creating a compelling email
client only to learn that it was really Gmail underneath AND there would be no
IMAP support…the conversation made our misalignment apparent).</p>
<h2>Decentralization</h2>
<p>As my concerns about online privacy grew, so did my interest in
decentralization. The core premise of decentralization is basically
self-hosting any online service you may need, yourself. The open-source
community is <em>fantastic</em> for that. You may find some projects with plenty of
issues in their git repos and design/code quality of varying degrees of
excellence but they are <em>all</em> great bases to get started from.</p>
<p>One of my favorite aspects of decentralization is discovering a codebase
someone shared eons prior and finding out that a particular function (or even
the entire codebase) fits in perfectly with whatever I&#39;m working on. It
sometimes feels like spelunking. You&#39;ll never know what you find but treasures
await! My other favorite aspect of it is knowing that <em>I</em> am in control of my
data. There&#39;s no ambiguity there. I don&#39;t have to trust a third-party, I can
trust myself. After all, I wrote the code (or adapted it after I read through
it).</p>
<p><em>A key aspect of decentralization that scares non-tech-savvy people is
self-hosting.</em> Of course I can say that it&#39;s no big deal but that&#39;s because
I&#39;ve been doing this for years. Some tech-savvy people just don&#39;t want to deal
with server updates and the like. I totally get that because maintenance <em>can</em>
be a drag. You&#39;ve really got to decide what you want for yourself. Personally,
I think self-hosting is important and I advise everyone to try it at least
once. Even if it&#39;s just to get over that fear of purchasing (well, <em>leasing</em>)
a $5/month server from DigitalOcean<a href="https://www.digitalocean.com">5</a> or Exoscale<a href="https://www.exoscale.com">6</a> to hack on and test
things with.</p>
<p>Here&#39;s a list of things I self-host:</p>
<ul>
<li>CMS: Noto<a href="https://git.inc.sh/IdeasNeverCease/Noto">7</a> (super simple Markdown-based &quot;CMS&quot; I created that runs the blog
you&#39;re reading right now)</li>
<li>Email: Mail-in-a-Box<a href="https://mailinabox.email">8</a> (this is <em>super</em> simple to setup)</li>
<li>Git: Gitea<a href="https://gitea.io">9</a> (MUCH lighter than GitLab and more customizable too)</li>
</ul>
<p>If self-hosting is not your thing, you can sign up and/or join servers other
people have created. For example, Mastodon<a href="https://mastodon.social">10</a> is a decentralized Twitter-like
social network. You can fire up your own Mastodon instance or you can sign up
for one and start chatting with people. I&#39;m taking the opposite approach with
the social network I&#39;m developing but I intend to add decentralized features
to it, like PubSub support.</p>
<p>Speaking of which, I am working on a social network and an analytics service
because 1) I was not able to find exactly what I was looking for, and 2) if
you want something done right you gotta do it yourself. I&#39;ve already detailed
my reasons for starting a social network<a href="/2017-12-30-who-creates-social-networks.txt">11</a> before but I never published
anything about the analytics service.</p>
<p>Plain and simple, I abhor trackers. However, I enjoy viewing stats that tell
me how many people visit my site, the most popular link visited today, and so
on. I was using Gauges<a href="https://gaug.es">12</a> prior to creating Chew<a href="https://chew.sh">13</a> and one of my tech-savvy
friends expressed to me that while he knows who I am and can trust me, he
wasn&#39;t going to go through the trouble of whitelisting my blog. I don&#39;t blame
him, the advertising industry is to blame. With more people utilizing ad
blockers, how would anyone get accurate analytics? I realized that I could
utilize the middleware function in Express<a href="https://expressjs.com">14</a> to get my analytics. I may go
deeper into my thought-process and inspiration for Chew at a later date but
for now, you check it out<a href="https://chew.sh">13</a> and use it in your own apps!</p>
<h2>What now?</h2>
<p>Getting your family, friends, and community onboard with what you&#39;ve just
learned is an uphill battle. You can lead by example though, so <em>do not feel
discouraged</em> if/when they don&#39;t care about the privacy implications of staying
with w̶e̶l̶l̶deceptively-designed services. We did not arrive at this clusterfuck
of invasiveness and moral ambiguity overnight…it took some time and it will
likely take some time to free ourselves from it.</p>
<p>Good luck. 🕸</p>
<hr>
